proof_skeleton_nl: Split into two genus ranges. In the low-genus range g < m-1, use the multiplicity obstruction to show A_{m,g} is empty, hence N(m,g)=0 and the inequality is immediate. In the range g >= m-1, define a canonical child map by deleting the least effective generator of each numerical semigroup S in A_{m,g}. The existence of an effective generator makes this map well-defined, and deleting such a generator preserves multiplicity while increasing genus by exactly one. Parent recovery from the child's Frobenius number yields injectivity of this map. Finally, an injection A_{m,g} -> A_{m,g+1} implies N(m,g) <= N(m,g+1). Combining the two ranges proves the theorem for all g >= 0.

steps.derives: For every integer m >= 2 and every integer g with 0 <= g < m-1, one has N(m,g)=0.
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the concluding clause of L1.

steps.derives: For every integer m >= 2 and every integer g >= m-1, the rule S ↦ C(S), where C(S)=S\{e(S)} and e(S) is the least effective generator of S, maps A_{m,g} into A_{m,g+1}.
steps.trivial_justification: From L6, whenever S is a numerical semigroup with multiplicity m and genus at least m-1, C(S) is well-defined, has multiplicity m, and satisfies g(C(S))=g(S)+1. Specializing to S in A_{m,g} gives C(S) in A_{m,g+1}.

steps.derives: For every integer m >= 2 and every integer g >= m-1, the canonical map C : A_{m,g} -> A_{m,g+1} is injective.
steps.trivial_justification: This is precisely the assertion of L7.

steps.derives: For every integer m >= 2 and every integer g >= m-1, one has N(m,g) <= N(m,g+1).
steps.trivial_justification: A3 provides an injective function A_{m,g} -> A_{m,g+1}; L8 converts that injection into the cardinality inequality.

steps.derives: If m >= 2 and g >= 0 satisfy g < m-1, then N(m,g) <= N(m,g+1).
steps.trivial_justification: By A1, N(m,g)=0. Since N(m,g+1) is a cardinality, it is a nonnegative integer. Therefore 0 <= N(m,g+1), so N(m,g) <= N(m,g+1).

steps.derives: For every integer m >= 2 and every integer g >= 0, the number N(m, g) of numerical semigroups with multiplicity m and genus g satisfies N(m, g) <= N(m, g + 1).
steps.trivial_justification: Fix arbitrary integers m >= 2 and g >= 0. Either g < m-1 or g >= m-1. In the first case, A5 gives N(m,g) <= N(m,g+1). In the second case, A4 gives N(m,g) <= N(m,g+1). Since one of these two cases always holds, the claimed inequality is true for all m >= 2 and g >= 0.
